metadata.title: How much more expensive is the basket? | Everyday Economics
metadata.description: See how prices and incomes have moved, using quarterly ABS CPI and WPI for Australia and annual World Bank CPI and GDP per capita for six economies.

hero.eyebrow: A short economics lesson on price changes
hero.titleLine1: How much more expensive is the basket?
hero.intro: Compare two national quarterly indices over the same period: one tracks prices paid by households, the other tracks wage prices for a comparable mix of jobs. Rebase each series to 100 at the starting quarter, then see where they go.
hero.noteBody: Index levels depend on their reference period. Here we compare percentage changes, not the raw index points.

learning.title: The two lines answer different questions
learning.cpiTitle: How much more do household purchases cost overall?
learning.cpiBody: The CPI summarises price changes for goods and services households commonly buy, weighted by their importance in household spending. The Australian national series is a weighted average of the eight capital cities. Every household has a different basket, so the CPI is not your personal bill.
learning.wpiTitle: How have wage prices changed for similar jobs?
learning.wpiBody: The WPI tracks wage price changes for a comparable mix of jobs, aiming to exclude changes in job content, quantity and quality. This chart uses the original index for total hourly rates of pay excluding bonuses. It does not describe any person's pay, hours, bonuses or after-tax income.
learning.normalizeTitle: Different reference periods: compare percentage changes
learning.normalizeBody: An index reference period is just the starting point for its scale. We set both selected starting quarters to 100; later values show each series' change from that point. The gap between the lines is the difference in cumulative index growth, not a difference in any person's purchasing power.
learning.normalizeLink: The comparable measures are trends and changes over the selected period.

world.realLabel: GDP per capita after CPI inflation
world.realInitial: Nominal GDP per capita multiple ÷ CPI multiple.
world.realUpDetail: Nominal GDP per capita grew faster than CPI; the gap between the lines is {gap} percentage points.
world.realDownDetail: Nominal GDP per capita did not keep up with CPI; the gap between the lines is {gap} percentage points.
world.realSameDetail: The two measures moved by about the same amount.
world.calculationNote: Change after CPI inflation = (end ÷ start nominal GDP per capita) ÷ (end ÷ start CPI) − 1. Over long periods this differs a lot from the percentage-point gap: if prices double and nominal income triples, the gap is 100 points, but income after inflation is only 50% higher.
world.cpiBody: The World Bank republishes consumer price indices from the IMF's International Financial Statistics as annual averages, all set to 2010 = 100. Each country builds its own basket and method, so compare each country's changes rather than index points.
world.incomeTitle: Nominal GDP per capita (current local currency)
world.incomeBody: All final goods and services produced in a year, valued at that year's prices and divided by the population. Like CPI it is not adjusted for inflation, so the two can be compared; but it includes company profits and government revenue, so it is not household wages or disposable income.
world.noteTitle: What to keep in mind here
world.note.AUS: Above are the ABS quarterly CPI and WPI; this section uses World Bank annual data. Annual CPI is a yearly average, so it will not match any single ABS quarter exactly. GDP per capita is not a wage measure either, so it answers a different question from the WPI above.
world.note.USA: At the time of this snapshot the World Bank has published US CPI only up to 2024, so the US years end in 2024.
world.note.KOR: Korean data begin in 1960. Over long spans both lines rise many times over and flatten the recent decades, so a shorter period is easier to read.
world.note.JPN: Japan's CPI was mostly flat or slightly falling from the late 1990s to the early 2010s, and nominal GDP per capita actually fell over that period. Try 1997 to 2012.
world.note.SGP: Singapore's GDP includes large profits earned locally by foreign-owned firms, so GDP per capita can sit well above what residents actually receive. Read it as output per person.
world.note.CHN: World Bank CPI for China starts in 1986, so China's years begin there. Figures cover mainland China.
